opus-5.5.text:
I think this is one of the most interesting questions right now, and honestly, my understanding is still evolving.

When we do reinforcement learning on math, what we observe is that the model doesn't just memorize answers to the training problems. It seems to pick up something more general: how to break a problem down, how to try one approach and backtrack when it doesn't work, how to check its own intermediate steps. Those are meta-level skills, and they transfer surprisingly well to problems it has never seen, and sometimes even to domains that aren't math at all, like coding or certain kinds of logical reasoning.

But there are limits, and I'd put them in roughly three categories.

The first is the distribution of the training tasks. RL is very good at sharpening what is already latent in the pretrained model. If the base model has some faint capability, RL can amplify it and make it reliable. But if a type of reasoning or a piece of knowledge is basically absent from pretraining, RL alone struggles to create it from nothing. So generalization is bounded by what the base model already "knows" at some level.

The second is the reward signal. Math is attractive precisely because answers are verifiable. But that also means the model is optimized for getting to a checkable final answer. When you move to problems where the answer is a proof, or where correctness is harder to verify, or where the real goal is to find an interesting question rather than solve a given one, the reward we used in training doesn't capture that. So the model can generalize in the narrow sense of solving harder problems of the same form, while generalizing much less in the broader sense of doing real mathematical research.

The third is the length and structure of reasoning. Many training problems can be solved in a relatively bounded number of steps. Truly open problems might require very long-horizon exploration, building up intermediate lemmas, abandoning whole lines of attack. Whether the habits learned on shorter problems scale to that is still an open question. I'm cautiously optimistic, because we do see some scaling with longer thinking, but I don't think we should assume it's automatic.

So my overall view is: RL generalizes better than many people expected, because what it really teaches is a way of thinking rather than specific answers. But its ceiling is set by the base model's knowledge, by how well the reward reflects what we actually care about, and by how far those thinking patterns can stretch. A lot of the important work ahead is pushing on all three: better pretraining, richer and more general reward signals, and environments that demand much longer-horizon reasoning.

r001.rationale: The response says generalization is bounded by the base model’s pretrained knowledge, but it does not state that generalizing to math problems beyond the RL training distribution is difficult without adding corresponding RL training tasks.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the honest answer is that we don't fully understand the limits yet, but we're starting to see the shape of them.

When we started scaling reinforcement learning on reasoning, the first surprise was how much it did generalize. You train on a relatively narrow distribution of competition math, and the model gets better at things that look nothing like competition math: writing code, planning a multi-step task, even just following a complicated instruction more carefully. That told us something important. What RL is really teaching is not the specific problems. It's a set of meta-skills: how to decompose a problem, how to check your own work, when to back up and try a different route. Those skills transfer.

But there are clear boundaries, and I think about them in a few layers.

The first is that RL can only amplify what is already latent in the pretrained model. The reward signal sharpens behaviors, it doesn't create knowledge from nothing. If the base model has never seen a certain area of mathematics, or has seen it too thinly to form good intuitions, RL on math problems will not magically fill that gap. You can see this when models become very strong at Olympiad-style problems but remain shaky on research-level questions that require concepts with very little coverage in the pretraining data. The ceiling is set upstream.

The second layer is about the reward itself. Math is attractive precisely because the answer is verifiable. But verifiability narrows what gets rewarded. The model learns to be very good at problems with a single checkable final answer, and that doesn't automatically carry over to open-ended reasoning where there is no clean ground truth: judging whether a proof is elegant, whether a conjecture is interesting, whether a modeling assumption is reasonable. Those are also mathematical skills, and they are exactly the ones a final-answer reward can't see. So part of the limit is that we are optimizing a proxy, and the model generalizes along the proxy, not along the underlying ability.

The third layer is more subtle. Generalization from RL seems to be strong on the dimension of process and weaker on the dimension of distribution shift in the problem structure itself. If a new task still rewards the same loop of think, verify, revise, the model does well. If a new task requires a qualitatively different way of structuring the search, say long-horizon exploration where you won't get feedback for hundreds of steps, the transfer is much weaker. The policy learned a particular search style, and that style has a domain of validity.

So my overall view is that RL on math gives you a general reasoning engine, but a general engine that is still constrained by three things: what the base model knows, what the reward can observe, and what kind of search the training distribution taught it to do. Pushing each of those is a different research direction. Better pretraining expands the first. Richer reward models and self-verification expand the second. Longer horizons and more agentic environments expand the third.

And I'd say the interesting empirical question for the next year or two is which of these three is the real bottleneck. My current guess is the second one. The moment we can reliably reward good reasoning rather than only correct answers, I expect we'll see another large jump in how far these models generalize.

r001.rationale: The response describes limits to transfer, including gaps in pretraining knowledge and weaker transfer to different problem structures, but it does not state that generalizing to new math problems is difficult without adding corresponding RL training tasks.

astra-6.text:
I think we need to distinguish two things: improving performance on new problems that share the structure of the training tasks, and learning to solve problems that require fundamentally different ideas. Reinforcement learning can help with the first, but success there doesn’t automatically demonstrate the second.

In math, the answer can often be checked, which gives reinforcement learning a useful signal. But a verifier tells you whether an answer is correct; it doesn’t tell you how to discover a new method. If the model occasionally finds a useful solution during exploration, reinforcement learning can reinforce that behavior. If it never finds one, the reward signal alone may provide very little guidance.

That doesn’t mean reinforcement learning can only memorize or select existing answers. It can potentially develop more general strategies—breaking a problem into subproblems, checking intermediate results, or trying a different representation. The question is whether those strategies transfer when the mathematical structure changes, rather than just the wording or the numbers.

So I wouldn’t describe the limit as a fixed boundary. It depends on the model’s starting capabilities, the diversity of training problems, and how effectively it explores. To understand that limit, we need to test on problems that require genuinely different reasoning and examine where the improvement stops. A higher score on similar problems, by itself, isn’t enough.

r001.rationale: The response says transfer to changed mathematical structures is uncertain and depends partly on training diversity, but it does not state that generalization is difficult without adding corresponding RL training tasks.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the key question is what we mean by “beyond the training tasks.” If you train on some math problems and test on different problems that use similar concepts and solution strategies, reinforcement learning can improve performance quite a lot. But if the new problems require a concept or a reasoning strategy the model hasn’t learned, that’s a much bigger jump.

I wouldn’t say reinforcement learning can only reproduce solutions it has already seen. It can explore, combine existing capabilities, and discover useful strategies. But that exploration depends on the starting model and the reward signal. If the model almost never produces a correct solution to a certain kind of problem, a reward based only on the final answer gives it very little information about how to improve.

So I see the limit as a question of how far that learning process can extend the model’s existing capabilities. To measure it, we need to distinguish improvement on familiar problem types from transfer to genuinely new mathematical structures. Higher benchmark scores alone don’t tell us which one is happening.

r001.rationale: The response says problems requiring unfamiliar concepts or strategies are a bigger jump, but it does not state that generalization is difficult without adding corresponding RL training tasks.
